subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Pressure as perpendicular force per unit area
Count particles with the amount of substance
The ideal gas as a model of real gases
From the three gas laws to PV/T = constant
The ideal gas law in two forms
Pressure from molecular collisions and P = ⅓ρv²
Internal energy of an ideal monatomic gas
When a real gas behaves like an ideal gas

questions.q: A sealed container holds a gas at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Which statement about this pressure is correct?
options: The gas presses mainly on the base of the container, because gas pressure acts downwards.
Pressure is a vector, so the pressures acting on opposite walls of the container cancel out.
The gas exerts a force of 1.0 × 10⁵ N on each wall, whatever the area of that wall.
The gas pushes perpendicular to every wall, exerting 1.0 × 10⁵ N on each square metre of wall.
optionWhy: A student who thinks gas pressure is caused by the weight of the gas picks this. The weight of the gas in a container is negligible; the pressure comes from molecules colliding with every wall, and it is the same on the top, sides and base.
A student who treats pressure as a vector picks this. Pressure is a scalar. The FORCES on opposite walls are opposite in direction, but the pressure on each wall is the same positive 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.
A student who treats pressure and force as the same quantity picks this. The force depends on the area: F = PA, so a wall of 0.20 m² receives 2.0 × 10⁴ N and a wall of 2.0 m² receives 2.0 × 10⁵ N.

Pressure is force per unit area, so F = PA: every 1 m² of wall receives a force of 1.0 × 10⁵ N, directed perpendicular to the wall. Because the molecules move randomly in all directions, this is true for the top, the sides and the base alike.
questions.explain: Pressure is force per unit area, so F = PA: every 1 m² of wall receives a force of 1.0 × 10⁵ N, directed perpendicular to the wall. Because the molecules move randomly in all directions, this is true for the top, the sides and the base alike.
questions.working: P = F/A, so F = PA = (1.0 × 10⁵ Pa)(1 m²) = 1.0 × 10⁵ N on each square metre, perpendicular to the wall.

questions.q: A cylinder contains 0.64 kg of oxygen gas, which consists of O₂ molecules. The molar mass of oxygen atoms is 16 g mol⁻¹, and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. How many oxygen molecules are in the cylinder?
optionWhy: The molar mass of O₂ is 2 × 16 = 32 g mol⁻¹ = 0.032 kg mol⁻¹, so n = 0.64 ÷ 0.032 = 20 mol. Then N = nN_A = 20 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.2 × 10²⁵ molecules.
A student who divides 0.64 kg by 32 g mol⁻¹ without converting units gets n = 0.020 mol, 1000 times too small. Convert first: 32 g mol⁻¹ = 0.032 kg mol⁻¹, giving n = 20 mol.
A student who treats the mass, 0.64, as the amount of substance multiplies it by N_A. The amount of substance is a count of particles in moles, found from n = m/M = 20 mol, not the mass itself.
A student who uses 16 g mol⁻¹ has used the molar mass of oxygen ATOMS. The gas consists of O₂ molecules, so its molar mass is 32 g mol⁻¹ and there are half as many molecules as this answer suggests.
questions.explain: The molar mass of O₂ is 2 × 16 = 32 g mol⁻¹ = 0.032 kg mol⁻¹, so n = 0.64 ÷ 0.032 = 20 mol. Then N = nN_A = 20 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.2 × 10²⁵ molecules.
questions.working: M(O₂) = 2 × 16 g mol⁻¹ = 32 g mol⁻¹ = 0.032 kg mol⁻¹. n = m/M = 0.64 kg ÷ 0.032 kg mol⁻¹ = 20 mol. N = nN_A = 20 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 1.2 × 10²⁵.

questions.q: Which of the following is an assumption of the kinetic model of an ideal gas?
options: All the molecules move with the same speed, which increases with temperature.
Molecules lose a small amount of kinetic energy in every collision with one another.
Molecules exert no forces on one another except during collisions.
The molecules are packed closely together and fill most of the container's volume.
optionWhy: A student who pictures every molecule with the same speed picks this. The model has molecules in random motion with a range of speeds; temperature fixes the average kinetic energy, which is why P = ⅓ρv² uses a MEAN square speed.

A student who thinks molecular collisions are like everyday inelastic ones picks this. The model assumes all collisions are elastic, so the total kinetic energy of the molecules is unchanged by collisions.

This is one of the model's assumptions. Together with point-particle molecules, elastic collisions of negligible duration and random motion, it defines the ideal gas; it also means an ideal gas has no intermolecular potential energy.

A student who pictures gas molecules as crowded picks this. The model treats the molecules as point particles whose total volume is negligible compared with the volume of the container; a gas is mostly empty space.
questions.explain: This is one of the model's assumptions. Together with point-particle molecules, elastic collisions of negligible duration and random motion, it defines the ideal gas; it also means an ideal gas has no intermolecular potential energy.

questions.q: For a fixed mass of gas, the ideal gas law PV/T = constant can be derived from three empirical gas laws. Which statement of those three laws is correct?
options: PV is constant at constant θ; V/θ is constant at constant P; P/θ is constant at constant V (θ in °C)
PV, V/T and P/T each stay constant (T in K), whatever happens to the remaining variable
PV is constant at constant T; V/T is constant at constant P; P/T is constant at constant V (T in K)
PV is constant at constant T; VT is constant at constant P; PT is constant at constant V (T in K)
optionWhy: A student who thinks any temperature scale will do picks this. V ∝ T and P ∝ T are proportionalities only when T is measured from absolute zero; with θ in °C, V/θ is not constant (it would be infinite at 0 °C).

A student who drops the conditions from the laws picks this. Each law holds only when the third variable is fixed: for example PV is constant only at constant temperature. If all three change, only PV/T is constant.

These are the three empirical laws, with temperature measured from absolute zero. Each is the special case of PV/T = constant in which one of P, V and T is held fixed, which is why they combine into the ideal gas law.

A student who assumes every gas law has the inverse form of Boyle's law picks this. Heating a gas at constant pressure makes it expand, so V increases with T (V/T constant), and heating at constant volume raises P (P/T constant).
questions.explain: These are the three empirical laws, with temperature measured from absolute zero. Each is the special case of PV/T = constant in which one of P, V and T is held fixed, which is why they combine into the ideal gas law.

questions.q: A rigid storage tank of internal volume 200 dm³ contains an ideal gas at a pressure of 3.00 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 27 °C. R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What amount of gas is in the tank?
options: 2.7 × 10² mol
2.4 × 10⁴ mol
2.4 × 10¹ mol
2.4 × 10³ mol
optionWhy: A student who uses 27 for the temperature gets an answer about eleven times too large. The ideal gas law needs absolute temperature: 27 °C = 300 K.
A student who substitutes V = 200 without converting dm³ gets an answer 1000 times too large. With R in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, V must be in m³: 200 dm³ = 0.200 m³.
Convert to SI: V = 200 dm³ = 0.200 m³ and T = 300 K. Then n = PV/(RT) = (3.00 × 10⁵ × 0.200) ÷ (8.31 × 300) = 24 mol = 2.4 × 10¹ mol.
A student who converts 200 dm³ to 20 m³ has divided by 10, the factor for lengths (10 dm = 1 m). For a volume the factor is cubed: 1 dm³ = 10⁻³ m³, so V = 0.200 m³.
questions.explain: Convert to SI: V = 200 dm³ = 0.200 m³ and T = 300 K. Then n = PV/(RT) = (3.00 × 10⁵ × 0.200) ÷ (8.31 × 300) = 24 mol = 2.4 × 10¹ mol.

questions.q: A flask of volume 250 cm³ contains an ideal gas at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 300 K. k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. How many molecules are in the flask?
optionWhy: A student who uses R instead of k_B has calculated PV/(RT) = 1.0 × 10⁻² mol, the amount of substance, not the number of molecules. R is the constant per mole; k_B is the constant per molecule.
A student who converts 250 cm³ to 2.5 m³ has divided by 100, the factor for lengths. For a volume the factor is cubed: 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³, so V = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m³.

A student who multiplies PV/(k_B T) by N_A treats the N in PV = Nk_B T as a number of moles. N is already the number of molecules; multiplying again by N_A gives an impossible 10⁴⁵ molecules in a small flask.

questions.q: Which statement correctly explains how a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container?
options: The weight of the molecules presses down on the container, mostly on its base.
Each molecule's momentum changes as it rebounds from a wall, so it exerts a force on the wall.
The molecules repel one another, and this repulsion pushes outwards on the walls.
Molecules give their kinetic energy to the walls, and this energy is the pressure.
optionWhy: A student who thinks gas pressure is caused by the weight of the gas picks this. The weight of a gas in a container is negligible, and the pressure is the same on the top and sides as on the base, because molecules strike every wall.

The wall exerts a force on each molecule to reverse its perpendicular velocity (a momentum change of 2mv for an elastic rebound), and by Newton's third law the molecule exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall. The total force from all collisions per unit area is the pressure.

A student who thinks of gas pressure as molecules pushing each other apart picks this. In the kinetic model there are no forces between molecules except during collisions; the pressure comes from momentum changes at the walls.

A student who confuses force with energy picks this. In an elastic rebound from a stationary wall a molecule keeps its kinetic energy; what changes is its momentum, and force is the rate of change of momentum.
questions.explain: The wall exerts a force on each molecule to reverse its perpendicular velocity (a momentum change of 2mv for an elastic rebound), and by Newton's third law the molecule exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall. The total force from all collisions per unit area is the pressure.

questions.q: A sealed, rigid container of ideal gas is heated. What happens to the pressure of the gas, and why?
options: It rises: the molecules expand when they are heated, so they strike the walls more often.
It stays the same: the number of molecules per unit volume has not changed at all.
It rises: faster molecules hit the walls more often, each with a greater change in momentum.
It rises: the molecules collide more often with one another, and so push harder on the walls.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the molecules themselves grow when heated picks this. Molecules do not change size; heating raises their speed, and that is what increases the frequency and momentum change of collisions.

A student who thinks pressure depends only on how crowded the molecules are picks this. Pressure also depends on molecular speed (P = ⅓ρv²); at constant volume it rises in proportion to the kelvin temperature.

The volume and number of molecules are fixed, but heating raises the mean square speed. Faster molecules cross the container more often, so they strike each wall more frequently, and each collision reverses a larger momentum. Both effects raise the force per unit area.

A student who thinks pressure comes from molecules pushing on one another picks this. Collisions between molecules do not push on the walls; the pressure comes from the momentum change of molecules rebounding from the walls, which increases because they move faster.
questions.explain: The volume and number of molecules are fixed, but heating raises the mean square speed. Faster molecules cross the container more often, so they strike each wall more frequently, and each collision reverses a larger momentum. Both effects raise the force per unit area.

questions.q: A container holds 8.0 g of helium, a monatomic gas of molar mass 4.0 g mol⁻¹, at 27 °C. Treat helium as an ideal gas. R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the internal energy of the helium?
optionWhy: A student who calculates nRT = 4986 J has left out the 3/2. nRT equals PV, which is two thirds of the internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas: U = (3/2)nRT.
A student who uses 27 for the temperature gets an answer about eleven times too small. U is proportional to the absolute temperature, 300 K.
A student who uses the mass, 8.0, as the amount of substance gets four times the correct value. The amount of substance is n = m/M = 8.0 g ÷ 4.0 g mol⁻¹ = 2.0 mol.

questions.q: Under which conditions does a real gas behave most nearly as an ideal gas?
options: High temperature, low pressure and low density
Low temperature, low pressure and low density
High temperature, high pressure and high density
Any temperature and pressure, provided the gas is helium
optionWhy: At low pressure and density the molecules are far apart, so their own volume and their mutual attractions are negligible; at high temperature their kinetic energy is large compared with the intermolecular potential energy. These are the conditions assumed by the model.

A student who thinks slower molecules interact less picks this. At low temperature the molecules' kinetic energy is small compared with the intermolecular potential energy, so attractions matter more and the gas deviates more, eventually liquefying.

A student who thinks more collisions means a better fit to the kinetic model picks this. At high pressure and density the molecules are crowded, so their volume and attractions are no longer negligible, and the gas deviates from ideal behaviour.

A student who thinks some gases are ideal gases picks this. Whether a real gas approximates an ideal gas depends on the conditions; helium is close to ideal at ordinary conditions but deviates at high pressure and near 4 K, where it liquefies.
questions.explain: At low pressure and density the molecules are far apart, so their own volume and their mutual attractions are negligible; at high temperature their kinetic energy is large compared with the intermolecular potential energy. These are the conditions assumed by the model.
